# Introduction

In many developing economies, higher agricultural productivity raises rural incomes, improve food security, and reduce poverty. For households that depend on farming, productivity determines how much output can be generated from the land, labour, capital, and other resources available to them, with direct implications for farm income and livelihoods. Productivity growth provide an important way through which agriculture support economic development and improve rural welfare [@WorldBank2007; @Timmer2009]. Where land is scarce, productivity gains depend on using existing resources efficiently and adopting improved technologies [@Fuglie2015; @FAO2022]. Differences in farmers’ ability to do so help explain variation in agricultural productivity and rural development.

The relationship between land ownership and agricultural productivity is often explained through investment incentives. Farmers with secure control over land have greater incentives to undertake investments whose returns extend beyond a single production cycle, such as soil improvement, irrigation, tree planting, and other land enhancing practices. Secure land rights may also encourage the adoption of technologies that require substantial upfront investment or have longer payback periods. Evidence from developing countries suggests that stronger land rights can increase investment and, in some settings, agricultural productivity, although the effects vary across institutional and production contexts [@Lawry2014; @Abdulai2010; @Fenske2011; @Abudikeranmu2025]. Consistent with this variation, some studies report higher productivity among farmers with secure land rights [@Kousar2018; @Selejio2022; @Nouf2023], while others show that the effects depend on tenure arrangements and the conditions under which farmers operate. Secure land rights may encourage investment without generating corresponding productivity gains when farmers face constraints in accessing credit, inputs, technology, or markets [@Lawry2014]. These mixed findings also raise a measurement issue, since land ownership extends beyond whether a farmer owns land. A binary measure overlook differences in documentation, rights to sell, transfer, lease, or pledge land, as well as differences in how land was acquired. Land obtained through purchase, inheritance, family allocation, or customary arrangements  provide different levels of security and control over its use.

This institutional variation is particularly important in Ghana, where customary and statutory land tenure systems operate alongside each other. These systems provide farmers with different forms and degrees of security and control over land. Evidence from northwestern Ghana documents substantial variation in customary land rights and tenure security among smallholder farmers [@Nara2021]. Customary institutions also continue to shape the allocation, use, and transfer of land alongside formal land administration [@Ubink2007; @Peters2022]. Such differences in land rights affect farmers’ incentives to invest, adopt technologies, and manage land over time. A binary measure of ownership can therefore conceal institutional differences that are relevant to agricultural production.The way farmers acquire land also shapes the rights and obligations associated with its use. Purchase, inheritance, family allocation, rental, and sharecropping can provide different levels of tenure security, control, and claims over the returns from land based investments. These differences influence how farmers manage land and make production decisions [@Lawin2018], with recent evidence showing variation in agricultural productivity across different modes of land access [@Akpo2024]. Land ownership therefore encompasses different forms of access and control, each with potentially distinct implications for agricultural performance.

Productivity effects of land tenure arrangements also depend on the technology available to farmers and how efficiently they use it. Agricultural performance reflects both the production possibilities provided by available technology and farmers’ ability to convert inputs into output. Farmers therefore differ in productivity because they operate with different technologies, use similar technologies with different levels of efficiency, or both. In production frontier analysis, technology endowment captures differences in the production possibilities available to farmers relative to the best available technology, while technical efficiency captures how effectively farmers use the technology at their disposal [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008]. Meta frontier studies apply this distinction to separate technology gaps from efficiency differences across production systems and farmer groups [@TweneboahKodua2022; @Birhanu2022; @Uddin2014]. Evidence from Ghana likewise shows that differences in technology and technical efficiency contribute to variation in agricultural performance across farmers and production environments [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2022; @Ansah2023].

Distinguishing between technology endowment and technical efficiency is important for interpreting productivity differences between landowners and non landowners. Higher productivity among landowners may reflect access to better production technology rather than more efficient resource use. Conversely, similar productivity across the two groups may conceal differences in technology and efficiency, as superior technology can offset lower technical efficiency. Aggregate productivity measures therefore cannot establish whether observed differences arise from technology endowment, technical efficiency, or both.

Farmers in sub-Saharan Africa operate with different production technologies and levels of technical efficiency across crops and production systems [@Tsiboe2019; @Tsiboe2022; @Asravor2024], with technology gaps contributing to differences in agricultural performance [@Tsiboe2021b; @Ansah2023]. The literature links land ownership to investment, productivity, and farm efficiency [@Lawry2014; @Fenske2011; @Abdulai2010; @Michler2015; @Ngango2021; @Schling2024], including resource use and investment in agricultural production [@Donkor2014; @Donkor2023; @Goldstein2008]. Yet it remains unclear whether productivity differences associated with land ownership reflect differences in technology, technical efficiency, or both. The owner–non owner distinction also overlooks differences in documentation, transferable rights, and modes of land acquisition that shape how farmers use land.

Ghana offers a useful setting to examine these dimensions because customary and statutory land institutions coexist, with farmers accessing land through diverse arrangements. Customary land rights and security vary substantially across farmers [@Nara2021], while customary institutions continue to shape land governance alongside formal institutions [@Ubink2007]. These institutional differences mean that land ownership does not represent a uniform set of rights or conditions of use. Examining these differences alongside technology endowment and technical efficiency can provide a clearer account of how land ownership relates to agricultural performance.

Building on this discussion, this paper examines how land ownership relates to agricultural performance in Ghana, focusing on whether landowners and non owners differ in productivity, whether such differences reflect technology endowment, technical efficiency, or both, and whether the relationship varies with documentation, transferable rights, mode of acquisition, and sharecropping intensity. The paper combines statistical matching with a Meta Stochastic Frontier (MSF) framework. Statistical matching compares landowners and non owners with similar observable characteristics, while the MSF framework separates differences in production technology from differences in technical efficiency. This approach builds on the meta frontier literature on producers operating under different technologies [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008; @Huang2014]. Together, the two methods provide a basis for identifying whether differences in agricultural performance are associated with the technology available to farmers, how efficiently they use it, or both.

The findings indicate that overall performance differs by less than one percentage point between landowners and matched non-owners, yet the two components of that aggregate move in opposite directions. Matched non-owners lie marginally closer to the meta-frontier technology (TGR of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$tgr$none), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$tgr$any), 3)`), while landowners attain higher technical efficiency relative to their own frontier (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$te$any), 3)` against `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$te$none), 3)`). Neither difference exceeds one
percentage point, and the residual meta-frontier efficiency gap of
`r fmt_num(100*abs(assert_present(objs$eff$mte$gap)), 1)` percentage points favours non-owners. Ownership is thus associated with neither superior access to technology
nor superior use of the technology available, an advantage on one component being
accompanied by a shortfall on the other.

Disaggregation by tenure form reveals differences that the aggregate overlooked, and these do not run in a single direction. Documented owners and holders of transferable rights lie
`r fmt_num(100*min(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 1)`
to
`r fmt_num(100*max(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 1)`
percentage points below matched non-owners in meta-frontier efficiency, the shortfall increasing as the rights held become more complete. Within rented, purchased, and family-allocated land the two components diverge: owners remain closer to the meta-frontier technology but fall
`r fmt_num(100*abs(max(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 1)`
to
`r fmt_num(100*abs(min(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 1)`
percentage points short in technical efficiency, which offsets that advantage. The
same pattern appears in graded form across sharecropping intensity, the owners'
shortfall reaching `r fmt_num(100*abs(assert_present(objs$shrcrp$high$mte)), 1)` percentage points where sharecropping is most intensive. The estimated ownership gap therefore depends on the dimension of tenure under consideration, and a binary owner/non-owner comparison averages two opposing components into an aggregate that registers little while both
remain active.


These findings have implications for policies concerned with land tenure and agricultural productivity. If ownership alone is not associated with a clear productivity advantage, formalizing ownership or expanding land titling should not automatically be expected to increase agricultural productivity. The productivity effects of stronger land rights may depend on whether farmers can also access credit, agricultural inputs, improved technologies, extension services, and functioning land and output markets. The results on land property-rights interventions suggests that such complementary conditions are important in determining whether stronger rights translate into productive investment and improved agricultural outcomes [@Lawry2014].Land policy should therefore consider not only the formal status of ownership but also the particular rights that farmers can exercise and the broader constraints affecting agricultural production.

The study contributes to the literature by moving beyond the conventional owner–non-owner classification by examining several dimensions of land ownership, including documentation, transferable rights, and mode of acquisition. This provide a detailed representation of the institutional conditions under which farmers operate. Also, it separates technology endowment from technical efficiency when examining agricultural performance which helps to identify whether differences between landowners and non-owners are associated with the production technology available to them or with how efficiently they use that technology. The study also combines statistical matching with a Meta-Stochastic Frontier framework to provide a more comparable assessment of performance differences while accounting for differences in observable characteristics and production technologies.

The remainder of the thesis is organised as follows. Chapter Two reviews the theoretical and empirical literature on land tenure, agricultural productivity, technology, and technical efficiency. Chapter Three presents the institutional context of land tenure in Ghana and describes the data used in the analysis. Chapter Four develops the empirical methodology, including the statistical matching procedure and the Meta-Stochastic Frontier framework. Chapter Five presents the empirical results, beginning with the aggregate comparison between landowners and non-owners and then examining differences across the dimensions of land ownership. Chapter Six discusses the findings and their implications for land and agricultural policy. The final chapter summarizes the main findings, draws conclusions, and discusses directions for further research.
